blocks.text: Afterword to the Record of Response and Practice Compendium

inline.s: The Record of Response opens its very first chapter with fortune and calamity, saying that man born into this world, if he does not obtain fortune, must obtain calamity — going out of one and into the other, with no place in between to stand. But it puts the word calamity first, to show that men, through delusion, accumulate evil and so encounter calamity, and that each time they awaken to the truth and turn their heart around and face goodness, they obtain fortune. When below it speaks of retribution, it does not say fortune and calamity but good and evil, to show that doing good is itself fortune and doing evil is itself calamity. Though the retribution of fortune and calamity comes several years or several decades later, yet the beginning of the matter and the planting of its cause had already lain in the several years or several decades before, when the thought of good arose or the thought of evil stirred. There is no one in the world who is willing to do evil; and so although a man be wicked, if you call him good he is pleased. It is precisely because he believes himself not to be evil that he rests content in evil and knows not to stop. The first item of evil in the chapter is “taking evil to be talent,” which means that in doing evil a man not only thinks himself not evil but also esteems himself able. Hence not only does he not know how to return and feel no shame, but he thinks no one is as able as he. Yet who does not know that Heaven sees him and men know him, and all detest him? But that he is pleased to be called good is the place where his moral nature is not yet drowned out. If he will but take this not-yet-drowned-out place and hold the Record of Response in hand from time to time, as a bright mirror set before him, he will catch a glimpse of his whole self, brows and beard all revealed, beauty and ugliness hard to conceal — and there is none who does not forthwith awaken and startled repent. As to doing good and obtaining fortune, it does not say “fortune’s retribution” but “good’s retribution,” to show that man’s doing good is originally to seek the restoration of his own original goodness, not that he does good in order to seek fortune. For Heaven rewards one who does not forget his original goodness, and bestows fortune on him because he can return to that first state. And as for man’s doing good, he himself does not know it is good; he only seeks to remove his accumulated habits so as to restore my original substance. Hence his offenses daily diminish and the original substance daily appears; and when the original substance reveals a single part, he looks upon himself ever more clearly and sees the whole nine parts of his fault. And when the original substance returns to nine parts, he feels the more intensely the uncleanness of that one part and finds it hateful; he deeply blames his own evil, and painstakingly scrapes it away, until only shame remains. Yet Heaven sees him and men know him, and none but respects his goodness. Hence in what he does and in the good that reaches others, heaven and men all approve it. But the good man only knows how to discipline his own person; he does not know that what he does is good. Therefore Jingzhu said: “Seeking to advance is a borrowed name; retreating to self-examination is the true method.” When I look upon the proofs and instances of ancient and modern gathered in this compendium and test them against my own person, I feel that since the beginning without beginning I have turned in the six paths and wandered in the sea of suffering, and that now, having escaped the three lower realms and attained human form, was hardest of all. And because from delusion rises falseness, and from falseness evil is done, unknowingly and unnoticing I have thrown away more than thirty years of time — truly a great pity. And what I did before I too believed I was not evil, and so was content in it and knew not to change, ran toward it and knew not to flee. Even what I cannot now cut away at one stroke and wash clean utterly is likewise from my thinking it a mere speck of harm, and that I will mend it slowly by and by. The evils listed in this chapter — in every one I have a share; the good items listed — of every kind I cannot do one. Whereupon I could not but be startled to fear, awaken to repent, and stand dismayed and self-bereft; and I could not keep from a grief that brought tears. Myself I saw as wholly foul and filthy, hateful and loathsome, crouching and ill at ease; and I thought how to wash and scrape and sweep it away. Then suddenly it came to me: “This is not the Record of Response — this is truly my life-saving king and bodhisattva.” Whereupon I burnt incense and bowed to it, honored and enshrined it with reverence, read and recited it at all times, and thought always to obey it; I praised it in every word, spoke of it to all I met, copied it, engraved it, printed it, and gave it away — and could not contain myself from doing so.

I, Wenran, went to sweep the grave of my ancestor the Lord Zhongxian and to return condolences at Jiangning, and there fell ill with malaria for more than a month. On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in a dream a man in feathered garments came to me. I wept and bowed to him, and presented him with a poem, whose last lines ran: “May I ask — did the little man once have a mother? Does she now stand on Lingfeng Terrace?” After a while I saw my late mother arrive. She said: “My son, are you ill with malaria? Recite the Record of Response of the Supreme One, practice it diligently, and also spread its teachings widely without slackening.” I wept and woke. The next day I sought the compendium from my friend Bao Mansu, and told him all my dream. Mansu said: “I have long promised to print an annotated edition of the Record of Response, but since it was hard to accomplish with my single strength I let it pass, and so I have been rebuked by the spirits, and my advancement has been frustrated; they have shown me warning in dreams again and again. Now I must make the effort to finish it.” Whereupon I joined heartily in the examination, and made a small contribution to the printing, to aid the other-worldly blessedness of my late mother. Each morning I first purified my mind and recited a full book. Looking back over my life, I felt shame, regret, disgrace, and fear all gather at once; and after several days the malaria indeed healed. Then I reflected that the Supreme One in great compassion delivers the deluded and the dull: fortune and calamity he shows to lie in one’s own calling-forth; good and evil he grounds in the rising of the mind. He instructs that the spirits stand upon man’s head and dwell within man’s body; that he of abundant virtue is not unmindful of even the smallest thing — hearing it one does not hear, looking at it one does not see. He teaches that Heaven bestows fortune for three years and sends down calamity for three years; that He who gives life lays its foundations according to each one’s stuff, raising the plantable and overturning the top-heavy. He points at the disease of the human heart and makes a medicine for the human heart; he lengthens man’s root of good and stops up man’s source of evil; he plants man’s field of blessings and plucks up man’s root of calamity. Such virtue and merit are beyond reckoning. Because of his compassionate teaching I have been able to hold in my hands this true text. Therefore I bow my head, weep, and compose this eulogy.
The Supreme One let down his precious teaching, / In pity for the race of men: / Fortune and ill from Heaven are not reaching, / All is made by the heart again.
Rise but a thought of good, not yet in deed, / The auspicious spirits follow near; / And when an evil thought has been sown, / The baleful spirits hold it dear.
Today men talk of doing good, / Yet cry their strength is weak; / Whoso clings to this opinion, / His heart is not good, so to speak.
As a poor and needy person, / Harbors a jewel within his coat; / Reckon its value, and it is worth / Numberless measures of silk and gold.
But if the poor man does not know / That a jewel is hidden there, / The Supreme One teaches three good things, / Named speech, sight, and action fair.
Has a mouth yet speaks no good — / All day must he sit in silence blest? / Has an eye but sees no good — / Never yet one that closed his eyes in rest.
Has a body yet does no good, / Toiling day and night in vain — / So by self-search, within, one knows: / To do good is not beyond our strain.
Only let the mind reach out, / And the measure of good is fully found. / In former days a beggar lad / Lived when bandits raged around.
The city guarded against spies / And would not let the beggar in; / So he lodged outside the walls, / Sleeping in a broken inn.
Suddenly the bandits came, / With countless horsemen and their sound; / The beggar rose up in his heart — / These thieves by night would storm the town.
The watchman’s clappers on the wall were spare, / The lamps burned dim, half-lit and low; / Because the people, weary, slept, / This realm would surely sink below.
I must take a byway there / And save this whole city’s life. / No sooner held that thought in mind / Than he ran below, crying strife.
The men on the wall were roused, / And drums and gongs all rang; / Arrows, stones, and matchlock shot, / Blindly through the dark they sprang.
The bandits in great terror fled, / Leaving their scaling ladders there. / Thus one beggar lad / Saved a million lives from care.
Now you who cry your strength is weak, / Who knew this beggar’s worth? / Look on this beggar again: / Can his merit be measured on the earth?
Therefore the lowest of the low / Can plant the highest of the high. / If the mind rises up to good, / No strength is wanting, no lack in the eye.
And there are those who have done wrong / And will not hold this scripture true; / Within their hearts they ever think, / “My offenses are deep and, heavy too.”
Speak no more of ghosts and spirits, / Causing yourself but added dread. / Do not think of the Supreme One’s teaching: / Repent and turn, and fortune is shed.
To reform is the seed of gathering good; / To repent is the root that kills our sin. / Since evil is made within the mind, / By the mind alone it is undone.
Take the water of a winter month, / Freezing, it becomes the ice; / And when the spring warmth comes again, / That same ice returns to water nice.
Thus know ice and water, / In nature are not two; / Again, like a clumsy chess-player / Whose game is half lost from the view.
If he meets a skillful player, / Who guides and teaches him his part, / If this man can trust and receive, / The end of the game sees victory art.
But if he is defeated still, / It must be that he would not believe. / An old monk there was of former days, / Who burned incense at Guan’s shrine and grieve.
His conduct was most pure and clean, / He bravely practiced every good. / When the bandits came, in a dream / The spirit spoke and its warning stood.
“Tomorrow you are doomed to die; / There is a robber riding white, / His name is Zhu Er — he is / The old enemy of a former life.”
“You must die by his hand.” He bowed / And said, “My life has known some good; / I beg compassion to rescue me.” / But the spirit said, “No help I could.
“If help there be, you must help yourself.” / At dawn the bell was rung; / A robber came into the hills / And the monk, seized, was made to lead among.
“What mountain holds your treasure? / What cave holds women fair? / Lead us there at once, / Or I’ll kill you then and there.”
Then the monk thought within himself: / “My karma says I must die; / If I lead them on to steal and ravish, / That is evil upon evil trie.”
“To plunder wealth and ravish women, / Is guilt heaped upon guilt; / Snow upon frost, and more — / A cangue laid upon a cangue-built.”
So rising, he called to the robber: / “I will no longer lead you on. / Are you not Zhu Er? / It is by your hand my life is gone.”
The robber was astonished / “How do you know my name? / Surely you are a holy monk.” / The monk told him of the dream and came.
Zhu Er thought within himself: / “The vengeance of wrong has no end. / That the spirit said it would not save, / Is itself the way that saves, my friend.
“You would not lead me on — / That is your own self-saving vow; / You and I dissolve the feud.” / So bowing, he departed now.
Thus know calamity can be turned; / The Supreme One speaks no lie. / Make haste and mend while you yet live, / Lest at death you grieve and sigh.
Reform and repentance are one with the mind, / So no offense but can be wiped away. / And there are those of weaker roots / Whose receiving and upholding do not stay.
Today they do a little good / And hope tomorrow for the pay; / They forget the Supreme One’s word: / “In the long, long time comes fortune’s day.”
The scripture the Supreme One spoke / Is like the rain from heaven above; / The good that men do in their lives / Is like the seed the earth must love.
The rain and moisture are but one, / But the soil is rich or poor; / The mandate received is thick or thin, / So swift or slow, and no more.
Plow and sow with all your might, / And in the autumn gather all; / If you sow too late and cast it off, / There is no harvest when the reapers call.
There are also those who do good, / Whom in the dark the spirits keep; / But fools, not knowing, wrongly say / That no great benefit runs deep.
They turn to doubt and slander, / Like a foolish, simple child / Standing beneath a tottering wall, / Playing with a fruit and wild.
Careless, he knows no fear; / His father rushes to his part, / Lifts the child to another place — / The wall falls; the child’s life is safe at heart.
Weeping, he says to his mother, / “Father snatched my fruit away.” / Again, like a man whose boat capsized / Who clutches a plank at break of day.
His wealth and goods are all cast off, / His clothes and bedding drowned too; / He bows in thanks to the saving spirits / And, vows fulfilled, returns to view.
But he whose boat did not capsize / Will speak no more of the spirit’s favor; / Therefore the great good man / With diligence and zeal does not waver.
Fortune in calm and ease is born, / Calamity in the dark is done away; / In the retribution of cause and effect / It is clearly told to men each day.
He who does good yet suffers pain / Is one whose good is not yet ripe; / When at last that good matures, / He will see the joy of the reward type.
I bow my head to the Supreme One, / Who delivers all the multitudes: / The mind gives birth to every good, / And good gives birth to every good’s goods.
If anyone receives this scripture, / Believes, and practices, and teaches abroad, / This is called giving of the Dharma / Whose merit no measure can afford.
In the yang month of the jia wu year of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing dynasty
On the longest day, Yao Wenran of Longshan bowed his head and respectfully composed this.
